item.title: UAT-10147 SPECTRE, Defender BTR.sys abuse, and Rust crate compromise
item.content:encoded:
Window: 20 Aug 10:00 → 20 Aug 14:00 UTC (4 hours)

Two popular Rust crates arrayref and append-only-vec compromised in Supply Chain Attack — Must Read

Two widely used Rust crates, arrayref and append-only-vec, were compromised to add a malicious build-time dependency that downloads and executes a remote payload when projects are compiled. Because arrayref has hundreds of millions of downloads, the incident represents a major Rust supply-chain compromise with broad potential impact.

  • Aikido detected that the Rust crates append-only-vec and arrayref were compromised by adding a dependency on the malicious package proc-macro1.
  • The proc-macro1 package downloads a remote payload during the build process and executes it on the developer’s machine, so compiling a project that pulls in either compromised crate can trigger infection.
  • The malicious build script targets Linux x86_64, Windows x86_64, macOS x86_64, and macOS aarch64 systems.
  • The affected package versions listed in the article are proc-macro-en 1.0.10, proc-macro1 1.0.107, append-only-vec 0.1.9, and arrayref 0.3.10.
  • The article lists 23.254.165.112:9089 as the payload delivery host and 23.254.165.112:443 as the command-and-control host passed to the executed payload.

Technologies: package-registry

Products: append-only-vec, arrayref, proc-macro1, proc-macro-en, proc-macro2, cargo, crates-io, aikido-safe-chain, aikido-intel, aikido-device-protection

Vendors: aikido, rust-project

UAT-10147: Chinese-speaking adversary integrates agentic AI into post-compromise operations — Must Read

Cisco Talos found that the Chinese-speaking cybercrime group UAT-10147 is using agentic AI tools to scale real intrusions against vulnerable Windows and Linux web servers, automating exploitation, reconnaissance, payload deployment, validation, persistence, and troubleshooting. The campaign shows how AI can lower the skill and time needed for complex post-compromise operations while increasing attack volume and efficiency.

  • Cisco Talos identified UAT-10147, a Chinese-speaking cybercrime group, targeting vulnerable Windows and Linux web servers globally across government, education, media, technology, and gaming sectors.
  • Talos found a target list on the actor’s command-and-control server containing approximately 170,000 URLs, which the actor split into 17 files of about 10,000 URLs each.
  • UAT-10147 used publicly disclosed vulnerabilities and offensive tools including Metasploit, ysoserial, PentestGPT, DeepAudit, and multiple privilege escalation exploits in its intrusion operations.
  • On Windows systems, the actor used scripts to download tools and payloads, add IIS directories to Windows Defender exclusions, deploy backdoors such as QuasarRAT, and establish persistence through scheduled tasks or rogue user accounts.
  • Talos assessed that UAT-10147’s use of AI-generated exploitation guidance, automation, validation workflows, and operational documentation helps scale complex attacks while reducing the expertise traditionally required for advanced post-compromise operations.

Technologies: operating-system, web-server, antivirus, ids-ips

Products: windows, linux-kernel, iis, microsoft-defender, powershell, asp-net, dotnet, zimbra-collaboration-suite, apache-nacos, telerik-ui-for-asp-net-ajax, metasploit-framework, ysoserial, pentestgpt, deepaudit, efspotato, quasarrat, meterpreter, snort, clamav

Vendors: cisco, microsoft, linux-kernel-project, zimbra, apache-software-foundation, progress, rapid7, sudo-project, frohoff

BTR Reforged: Weaponizing Defender’s Remediation Driver as a Kernel Operation Primitive — Should Read

Researchers found that Microsoft Defender’s signed Boot-Time Removal driver, BTR.sys, can be repurposed by an attacker with driver-loading privileges to perform kernel-level file and registry operations without exploiting a bug. The key takeaway is that trusted security components can become powerful living-off-the-land primitives, so defenders need behavioral detection around driver loading, ADS configuration, and unusual system-level changes.

  • Check Point Research reverse engineered Microsoft Defender’s Boot-Time Removal driver, BTR.sys, and found that its encrypted transaction format can be constructed to make the signed driver perform file and registry operations from kernel mode.
  • The driver reads an RC4-encrypted configuration blob from an Alternate Data Stream named :changelist, validates structures with a modified CRC-32 scheme, and supports actions including file deletion, directory deletion, file move, registry key deletion, registry value deletion, and registry value creation or modification.
  • The researchers built BTR_CLI, a proof-of-concept tool that extracts BTR.sys from MpEngine.dll, creates valid encrypted transactions, stages the driver as a service, and can trigger execution immediately or at boot.
  • The article demonstrates that staging BTR.sys as a Start=1 driver in the Boot Bus Extender group can run it during an early boot window before Defender’s main user-mode service starts, enabling deletion of Defender components and bypassing Tamper Protection in the tests described.
  • The article states that Microsoft MSRC did not classify the findings for immediate servicing because the technique requires existing administrative privileges, and recommends detection based on behavior such as ADS creation, unusual driver loading, service registry staging, and System-process file deletion.

Technologies: operating-system, antivirus, edr

Products: btr.sys, btr-cli, microsoft-defender, mpengine.dll, windows, sysmon, process-monitor, wdfilter.sys, msmpeng.exe

Vendors: microsoft, check-point-research

Perfect Authentication, Borrowed From a Real Mailbox — Should Read

A phishing email passed SPF, DKIM, DMARC, and ARC because it was sent from a genuinely compromised utility company mailbox, showing that perfect authentication does not mean a message is safe. The lure used a fake “attached document” link to an unrelated domain with a human-verification gate that blocked automated scanners.

  • Two mailboxes at a multi-site services organization received an “EFT payment summary” email in mid-July 2026 that passed SPF, DKIM, DMARC, and ARC validation.
  • The message was sent from a real employee mailbox at a real utility company through that company’s Microsoft 365 tenant, indicating the sender account was likely taken over rather than spoofed.
  • The email claimed a payment summary was attached, but no attachment existed, and its only link used the display text “REVIEW ATTACHED DOCUMENT HERE” while pointing to the unrelated domain engastando[.]us.
  • A fresh screenshot of the destination showed a human-verification interstitial with content delivery network branding and no visible username, password, or login form.
  • The landing domain was created in early April 2026, exactly 100 days before the email was sent, and the platform labeled the message as credential theft with 90 percent confidence.

Technologies: email-security, cloud-platform

Products: adaptive-ai, ironscales-platform, microsoft-365

Vendors: ironscales, microsoft, google

item.content:encoded:
Window: 20 Aug 02:00 → 20 Aug 06:00 UTC (4 hours)

Balancing AI Speed and Security in Financial Services — Optional

Financial services firms are rapidly adopting AI, but legacy infrastructure, shadow AI, data sprawl, and weak visibility are making governance and security lag behind. The key takeaway is that AI adoption needs integrated zero-trust visibility and controls so security can enable innovation without slowing it down.

  • Netskope surveyed 100 North American IT leaders in financial services and found that 62% of organizations have adopted managed third-party AI applications, 54% are building private internal AI applications, and 26% are experimenting with autonomous AI agents.
  • Only 1 in 100 surveyed organizations believe they can accelerate AI adoption without compromising security or operational integrity.
  • The top concerns identified in the research are shadow AI at 56%, loss of visibility into how AI makes decisions at 53%, and data sprawl and compliance risk at 43%.
  • Legacy architecture is cited by 60% of leaders as the main roadblock to new AI product launches, while 31% cite insufficient investment and 21% point to fragmented, siloed security tools.
  • The article argues that organizations should integrate AI governance into their existing security stack using a zero trust approach rather than relying on standalone AI monitoring tools.

AI pentesting evaluation checklist: What to look for in an AI pentesting vendor — Optional

AI pentesting vendors vary widely, so buyers should evaluate them with live, comparable tests focused on validated findings, workflow depth, code access, reliability, scope controls, and fit with release cycles. The key takeaway is to judge tools by proven exploitability and operational performance, not demos or reports alone.

  • The article says AI pentesting vendors should be evaluated by watching comparable live tests run, rather than by comparing final reports alone.
  • The checklist emphasizes validation and signal quality, including findings that are proven, reproducible, validated against a live system, and tied to actual exploit paths.
  • The article states that deeper AI pentesting should cover workflows, roles, application state, multi-step issues, and, when possible, source code or internal context.
  • The article says scope control and safety should be enforced technically during execution, including domain limits, production restrictions, automatic blocking of out-of-scope requests, and pre-flight checks.
  • The article cites Tyro Payments as a proof of concept where AI pentesting found about 30 issues in five and a half hours, while incumbent human penetration testers found five issues in approximately 15 days.

item.title: CVE-2026-60702 WebLogic Risk, BOFScale Tailnets, and AWSHound Cloud Attack Path Mapping
item.content:encoded:
Window: 19 Aug 14:00 → 19 Aug 18:00 UTC (4 hours)

Emerging Threat: (CVE-2026-60702) Oracle WebLogic Server Takeover via T3 and IIOP — Must Read

Oracle patched CVE-2026-60702, a critical WebLogic Server flaw that can let a low-privileged attacker with T3 or IIOP network access take over affected servers. Organizations should urgently identify exposed WebLogic instances, apply the August 2026 Oracle patches, and restrict T3/IIOP access on ports such as 7001 and 7002.

  • CVE-2026-60702 is a critical Oracle WebLogic Server Core vulnerability that allows a low-privileged attacker with network access over T3 or IIOP to compromise the server.
  • Oracle assigned CVE-2026-60702 a CVSS v3.1 base score of 9.9 and released fixes in its August 18, 2026 Critical Security Patch Update.
  • The affected Oracle WebLogic Server versions are 12.2.1.4.0, 14.1.1.0.0, 14.1.2.0.0, and 15.1.1.0.0.
  • The article says T3 is enabled by default and shares the same listener as the HTTP interface, so WebLogic systems exposed on TCP/7001 or TCP/7002 may also expose T3.
  • Recommended actions include inventorying WebLogic instances, confirming versions, restricting T3 and IIOP access, blocking TCP/7001 and TCP/7002 from untrusted networks, auditing accounts, and monitoring logs for unexpected T3 and IIOP connections.

Technologies: web-server, iam

Products: oracle-weblogic-server, oracle-fusion-middleware, oracle-identity-manager, oracle-soa-suite, oracle-webcenter, peoplesoft, oracle-e-business-suite, cycognito-platform

Vendors: oracle, cycognito

BOFScale: A CDN-Fronted Tailnet from a BOF-PE — May Read

NetSPI’s BOFScale demonstrates a fully in-memory Tailscale/Headscale tailnet for red-team C2, running inside an implant with no driver, service, disk state, or child processes while tunneling DERP and control traffic as CDN-friendly WebSockets. The key defensive takeaway is to hunt for unexpected processes making WebSocket connections using Tailscale DERP or TS2021 subprotocols, in-memory BOFScale signatures, and unusual local SOCKS5 listeners.

  • BOFScale consists of three tools: a modified in-process Tailscale daemon called tailscaled, a C++ BOF-PE client called tailscale, and socksportfwd for forwarding local ports through the daemon’s SOCKS5 server.
  • The modified Tailscale implementation adds RFC 6455 WebSocket support for both DERP relay traffic and the TS2021 control channel so Headscale and DERP can sit behind CloudFront or Fastly.
  • The tailscaled BOF-PE runs in userspace networking mode with memory-only state, no TUN driver, no Windows service, no disk state, and no child processes after startup.
  • The Headscale Docker Compose stack uses Headscale’s embedded DERP relay, disables Logtail, keeps DERP traffic within the operator-controlled stack, and configures ephemeral implant nodes to be removed after ten minutes offline.
  • The article provides defensive guidance including YARA rules for BOFScale components, hunting for WebSocket upgrades with derp or ts2021 subprotocols, and checking for a SOCKS5 listener bound to 0.0.0.0:1080.

Technologies: vpn, proxy, cloud-platform, container-platform, web-server, remote-access

Products: bofscale, tailscale, tailscaled, headscale, headplane, cloudfront, fastly, docker-compose, caddy, apache-http-server, socksportfwd, ntlmrelayx, petitpotam, active-directory-certificate-services

Vendors: netspi, tailscale, headscale, amazon-web-services, fastly, docker, caddy, apache, microsoft

AWSHound: An OpenSource AWS OpenGraph Collector — May Read

AWSHound is a new open-source, read-only collector that turns AWS accounts or entire Organizations into BloodHound OpenGraph data so teams can find real AWS attack paths after evaluating IAM policies, SCPs, resource policies, boundaries, and conditions offline. Its key value is showing how individually boring AWS permissions can combine into practical privilege-escalation and cross-account compromise paths.

  • AWSHound is a free, self-hosted, read-only collector that turns an AWS account or AWS Organization into a BloodHound Community Edition OpenGraph dataset.
  • Before creating graph edges, AWSHound runs offline IAM policy evaluation so edges exist only when effective permissions resolve to Allow after SCPs, RCPs, permissions boundaries, and relevant resource policies are considered.
  • AWSHound has separate collect, process, emit, and ingest phases, with collection using only read actions such as List, Get, and Describe and emit producing a compressed graph.zip file for BloodHound ingestion.
  • The tool models AWS principals and resources as nodes and capabilities as edges, with only 36 of its 156 edge kinds marked as traversable for BloodHound pathfinding.
  • AWSHound currently includes collectors for IAM, Organizations, S3, KMS, SSM, EC2, Lambda, CloudFormation, and EKS, with future collectors planned for Bedrock, ECR, ECS, and CodeBuild.

Technologies: cloud-platform, iam, object-storage, secrets-manager, remote-access, container-platform, orchestration

Products: awshound, bloodhound-community-edition, bloodhound-enterprise-edition, bloodhound-opengraph, aws-iam, aws-organizations, amazon-s3, aws-key-management-service, aws-systems-manager, amazon-ec2, aws-lambda, aws-cloudformation, amazon-eks

Vendors: specterops, amazon-web-services, awshound

What Happens When Attackers Move Faster Than Healthcare Can Patch? — Optional

Healthcare organizations often cannot patch clinical systems quickly because fixes require vendor validation, testing, downtime planning, and regulatory or change-control approvals. As AI helps attackers find and exploit vulnerabilities faster, hospitals must focus on reducing exposure and limiting what attackers can reach while patches are delayed.

  • The health sector has long faced difficulty patching security issues because fixes to clinical systems can require vendor validation, hospital testing, scheduled downtime, and sometimes regulatory review.
  • AI tools are speeding up vulnerability reconnaissance, research, and exploit development, adding pressure to healthcare remediation processes.
  • Patching delays in healthcare are often lengthened by vendor dependencies, such as when an MRI system update must be validated by the vendor and approved through hospital change control.
  • Health-ISAC’s Frontier AI in the Health Sector report identifies delayed patching as one of the health sector’s defining exposures.
  • The article argues that hospitals may not control every part of the patch timeline, but they can limit what an attacker can do while an update is being rolled out.

When the Attacker Wears Your Logo: Detecting and Taking Down Impersonation at AI Speed — Optional

Brand impersonation is becoming faster and more convincing as attackers use AI to create fake domains, websites, profiles, ads, and communications that abuse customer trust without breaching company networks. Organizations need continuous monitoring and rapid takedown processes to reduce phishing, fraud, credential theft, and reputational harm.

  • Attackers can impersonate trusted brands by registering lookalike domains, cloning websites, creating fake executive profiles, publishing fraudulent job advertisements, and imitating customer-support accounts without breaching the legitimate organization.
  • The FBI’s 2025 Internet Crime Report recorded 1,008,597 complaints and $20.877 billion in reported losses, while business email compromise accounted for about $3.05 billion in reported losses from 24,768 complaints.
  • The FTC reported that consumers lost $3.5 billion to imposter scams in 2025, with nearly one in three fraud reports involving impersonation and nearly $1 billion lost to business impersonators alone.
  • AI has made impersonation faster, cheaper, and more convincing by helping attackers generate polished phishing messages, synthetic personas, cloned websites, and convincing voice or video content.
  • The article says rapid verification and takedown are important because fraudulent websites or social profiles can quickly steal credentials, collect personal information, or redirect payments.

Products: cyble-brand-intelligence, cyble-takedown-services

Vendors: cyble

item.title: Gogs CVE-2026-52813 RCE, DocuSign Linktree Phish, and AI-Scaled BEC
item.content:encoded:
Window: 19 Aug 10:00 → 19 Aug 14:00 UTC (4 hours)

Yet another RCE in Gogs, but it's fixed this time! — Should Read

Researchers found multiple Gogs vulnerabilities, including a path traversal flaw that could be chained into remote code execution via nested Git repositories and hooks, fixed in version 0.14.3. A separate Git HTTP authorization bypass remains incompletely patched, so users should apply the manual fix or avoid exposed smart HTTP access.

  • CVE-2026-52813 is a Gogs path traversal vulnerability in organization names created through the API that can write bare Git repositories outside the intended repository root.
  • The researchers chained the path traversal issue with a nested bare repository and an overwritten Git update hook to achieve remote code execution as the git user.
  • CVE-2026-52813 is fixed in Gogs version 0.14.3, and the article says users can check exposure by seeing whether their Gogs version is 0.14.2 or below.
  • CVE-2026-52810 is a Git HTTP authorization bypass in which Gogs can treat a push endpoint as a read operation when a crafted service parameter is used.
  • The article says the push authorization bypass fix is incomplete because uppercase variants such as git-RECEIVE-pack can bypass the check, and it provides a manual source code patch.

Technologies: source-control

Products: gogs, aikido-attack, git, notebookjs, bluemonday, mitmproxy

Vendors: gogs, aikido, notebookjs, microcosm-cc

The DocuSign Button That Went to a Link-in-Bio Page — Should Read

A DocuSign-themed phishing email spoofed a finance executive and hid its malicious call-to-action behind a legitimate Linktree page, making domain blocking and URL reputation ineffective. The key lesson is that behavioral signals, authentication gaps, and repeated template artifacts like a fake security code can be more useful indicators than infrastructure in SaaS-abuse phishing.

  • A DocuSign-styled completion notice sent to a multi-brand staffing company claimed to come from and be addressed to its own senior finance executive.
  • The “VIEW COMPLETED DOCUMENT” button resolved to a free Linktree profile rather than any DocuSign domain, lookalike domain, or attacker-owned domain.
  • The email body included a complete unrelated airline trip confirmation and payment receipt with eight genuine airline links that all scanned clean.
  • Email authentication showed SPF softfail, no DKIM signature, no DMARC policy, and an originating host with no reverse DNS entry, while the composite authentication verdict still passed.
  • IRONSCALES Adaptive AI scored the message at 84% confidence, quarantined it as phishing, and later detected the same template in additional mailboxes over five weeks.

Technologies: email-security

Products: docusign, linktree, adaptive-ai, dmarc-management-and-monitoring

Vendors: docusign, linktree, ironscales

Describing attacks with crime script analysis — Optional

Crime script analysis can make cyberattacks like business email compromise easier for non-technical audiences to understand by describing the attacker’s workflow as a narrative. This approach also helps defenders spot where AI may help attackers scale scams and where interventions can disrupt them.

  • Crime script analysis is a narrative-driven technique that describes attacks in human-readable stories that non-technical audiences can understand.
  • The article says crime script analysis can complement or provide an alternative format to tactics, techniques, and procedures and MITRE ATT&CK Attack Flow diagrams.
  • Using a business email compromise example, the article explains that AI can automate time-consuming preparatory work such as identifying targets and personalizing social engineering messages.
  • The article states that AI-assisted automation may shift business email compromise from higher-value fraud against a few targets to lower-value fraud against many targets.
  • The article identifies intervention points including fake canary organizations, AI provider detection of repeated reconnaissance and message generation patterns, email delivery controls, victim awareness, verified purchase orders, and payment delays.

Products: cyber-kill-chain, mitre-attack, attack-flow

Vendors: lockheed-martin, mitre

item.content:encoded:
Window: 19 Aug 00:00 → 20 Aug 00:00 UTC (1 day)

Emerging Threat: (CVE-2026-60702) Oracle WebLogic Server Takeover via T3 and IIOP — Must Read

Oracle patched CVE-2026-60702, a critical WebLogic Server flaw that lets low-privileged attackers with T3 or IIOP network access take over affected servers. Organizations should urgently identify exposed WebLogic instances, apply the August 2026 patches, and restrict T3/IIOP access from untrusted networks.

  • CVE-2026-60702 is a critical vulnerability in the Core component of Oracle WebLogic Server that allows a low-privileged attacker with network access over T3 or IIOP to compromise the server.
  • Oracle assigned CVE-2026-60702 a CVSS v3.1 base score of 9.9 and published it on August 18, 2026, as part of its August 2026 Critical Security Patch Update.
  • Oracle lists WebLogic Server versions 12.2.1.4.0, 14.1.1.0.0, 14.1.2.0.0, and 15.1.1.0.0 as affected.
  • T3 is enabled by default and shares the same listener as the HTTP interface, so WebLogic servers exposed on TCP/7001 or TCP/7002 may also expose the T3 listener.
  • The article recommends inventorying WebLogic instances, confirming versions, restricting T3 and IIOP access, blocking TCP/7001 and TCP/7002 from untrusted networks, auditing WebLogic accounts, and monitoring logs for unexpected T3 and IIOP connection attempts.

Oracle’s August 2026 Critical Security Patch Update fixes 925 CVEs with 943 patches, including 154 critical issues. Oracle Fusion Middleware and Oracle Hyperion received the most fixes, making rapid patch prioritization especially important for those environments.

  • Oracle released its August 2026 Critical Security Patch Update on August 18, addressing 925 unique CVEs in 943 security updates across 23 Oracle product families.
  • The update includes 154 critical patches across 151 CVEs, representing 16.3% of all patches.

77 Firefox Extensions Linked to Crypto Wallet and Credential Theft — Should Read

Researchers linked 77 Firefox extensions to a coordinated campaign dubbed “Offside Wallet Theft Factory,” with 40 confirmed malicious extensions stealing crypto wallet secrets, credentials, or clipboard data. The campaign used fake wallet interfaces, modified Rabby Wallet code, remote Supabase-controlled phishing loaders, and deceptive sports-score shell extensions that appear to serve as staging or repurposing infrastructure.

  • Socket Threat Research is tracking 77 Firefox extension identities linked through code reuse, cloned extensions, deceptive descriptions, add-on ID patterns, infrastructure, wallet impersonation, and version histories.
  • Extension-level analysis confirmed 40 extensions as malicious, while another 37 deceptive sports-score shell extensions showed no confirmed theft payloads in analyzed builds but were linked to the broader operation.
  • The malicious extensions impersonated OKX, Rabby Wallet, TronLink, and other Web3 products to steal recovery phrases, private keys, serialized keyrings, credentials, and clipboard data.
  • Seven extensions used threat actor-controlled Supabase projects as remote switches for phishing content, 15 exfiltrated wallet secrets through Cloudflare Workers, 13 modified Rabby Wallet builds exfiltrated serialized keyrings before local encryption, and five extensions stole credentials and clipboard data through hardcoded command-and-control infrastructure.
  • Historical versions showed several Firefox extension identities transitioning from sports-score shells or benign-looking utilities into wallet-stealing extensions under the same Firefox IDs.

Technologies: browser, package-registry, cloud-platform

Products: firefox, firefox-add-ons, supabase, cloudflare-workers, cloudflare-pages, okx-wallet, rabby-wallet, tronlink, api-sports

Vendors: mozilla, supabase, cloudflare, okx, rabby, tronlink, api-sports

Yet another RCE in Gogs, but it's fixed this time! — Should Read

Researchers found multiple Gogs vulnerabilities, including a path traversal flaw that could be chained into remote code execution by abusing nested Git repositories and hooks; the RCE is fixed in version 0.14.3. A separate Git HTTP authorization bypass remains incompletely patched, so Gogs instances may still be at risk until a proper fix is applied.

  • Aikido researchers found a Gogs organization-name path traversal issue, CVE-2026-52813, that allowed repositories to be created outside the intended repository root when an organization was created through the API with a name containing '../' sequences.
  • The researchers escalated the path traversal into remote code execution by placing a bare repository inside an editable worktree, modifying its Git update hook through a normal Git push, and then triggering the hook by pushing to the nested repository.
  • Gogs version 0.14.3 fixes the reported remote code execution issue, and the article states that Gogs versions 0.14.2 and below are affected.
  • The article describes CVE-2026-52810, a Git HTTP authorization bypass where adding service=git-upload-pack to a git-receive-pack request could cause Gogs to treat a push as a read operation, allowing a read-only collaborator to write to certain repositories.
  • The article says the fix for CVE-2026-52810 is incomplete because an uppercase /git-RECEIVE-pack path bypass remains while the router later handles the route case-insensitively.

Technologies: source-control

Products: gogs, aikido-attack, notebookjs, bluemonday, git

Vendors: gogs, aikido, notebookjs, bluemonday

Grandoreiro goes north: From Brazil to Mexico with a new DLL sideloading campaign — Should Read

Grandoreiro remains active after 2024 disruption efforts, with a new campaign mainly targeting Mexico and Latin America by abusing the legitimate Duplicate Files Finder app for DLL sideloading. The loader uses extensive sandbox, VM, process, and geolocation checks before contacting C2 infrastructure, showing a strong focus on evading analysis.

  • Grandoreiro remains active despite major law-enforcement disruption efforts in 2024, with recent campaigns continuing to target users primarily in Latin America.
  • The analyzed campaign abuses the legitimate Duplicate Files Finder application to execute malicious code through DLL sideloading.
  • The initial Grandoreiro loader performs extensive anti-analysis checks, including sandbox detection, virtual machine artifact checks, process blacklisting, environment profiling, and geolocation checks before contacting its command-and-control infrastructure.
  • Telemetry from the last 30 days of June 2026 showed Grandoreiro activity concentrated in Latin America, with Mexico accounting for the largest share of observed samples.
  • The malware uses Google DNS-over-HTTPS to resolve a hardcoded command-and-control domain and then attempts to retrieve a second-stage payload over TCP port 6432.

AI-Agent-Driven Offensive Operation : Exposed Adversary Open Directory Reveals Autonomous Crypto-Theft Campaign Leading to Mass Wallet and Credential Compromise — Should Read

An exposed adversary open directory reportedly revealed an AI-agent-driven crypto-theft operation that autonomously targeted wallets and credentials at scale. The key takeaway is that attackers are using autonomous tooling to accelerate mass wallet and credential compromise.

The DocuSign Button That Went to a Link-in-Bio Page — Should Read

A DocuSign-themed phishing email spoofed a senior finance executive and hid its main lure behind a legitimate Linktree page, making URL reputation and domain blocking largely ineffective. The key detection signals were behavioral: SPF softfail, no DKIM or DMARC, a self-addressed executive sender pattern, and a repeated hard-coded security code across campaigns.

  • A DocuSign-styled phishing email claimed a nondisclosure agreement had been executed and presented a button labeled "VIEW COMPLETED DOCUMENT" with a fabricated security code.
  • The button led to a free Linktree profile rather than a DocuSign domain, and the legitimate Linktree platform scanned clean because it was not malicious infrastructure.
  • The message included a complete airline trip confirmation and payment receipt with eight genuine airline links, which acted as clean-looking filler content unrelated to the targeted organization.
  • The email spoofed a senior finance executive at a multi-brand staffing company, with SPF softfail, no DKIM signature, no DMARC record, and no reverse DNS entry for the originating host.
  • IRONSCALES Adaptive AI scored the message at 84% confidence, quarantined it automatically, and later caught the same template returning across three mailboxes and three affiliated brand domains over five weeks.

BOFScale: A CDN-Fronted Tailnet from a BOF-PE — May Read

NetSPI details BOFScale, an in-memory BOF-PE implementation of Tailscale that lets implants join a CDN-fronted Headscale tailnet over standard WebSockets without drivers, services, disk state, or child processes. The key defensive takeaway is to hunt for unusual in-process Go/Tailscale artifacts, permissive random named pipes, local SOCKS5 listeners, and WebSocket traffic using DERP or TS2021 subprotocols from non-Tailscale processes.

  • BOFScale consists of three tools: a modified in-process Tailscale daemon called tailscaled, a C++ BOF-PE client called tailscale, and a SOCKS5-based port forwarder called socksportfwd.
  • The modified Tailscale implementation makes both DERP relay traffic and the TS2021 control protocol use standard RFC 6455 WebSocket connections so Headscale and DERP can sit behind CloudFront or Fastly.
  • The tailscaled component runs inside the implant process with userspace networking, in-memory state, no kernel driver, no Windows service, no disk state, and no child processes after startup.
  • The included Headscale Docker Compose stack configures Headscale, embedded DERP, and Headplane to operate behind a CDN, with Logtail disabled, client-verified DERP, ephemeral node cleanup, and auto-approved subnet route advertisements.
  • The article provides defensive guidance including YARA rules for BOFScale components and network hunting for WebSocket upgrades using DERP or TS2021 subprotocols from unexpected processes.

AWSHound: An OpenSource AWS OpenGraph Collector — May Read

AWSHound is a new open-source, read-only collector that turns AWS accounts or entire Organizations into BloodHound OpenGraph data so teams can find real AWS attack paths after evaluating IAM policies, SCPs, resource policies, boundaries, and conditions offline. Its key value is showing how individually boring AWS permissions can combine into practical privilege-escalation and cross-account compromise paths.

  • AWSHound is a free, self-hosted, read-only collector that turns an AWS account or AWS Organization into a BloodHound Community Edition OpenGraph dataset.
  • Before creating graph edges, AWSHound runs offline IAM policy evaluation so edges exist only when effective permissions resolve to Allow after SCPs, RCPs, permissions boundaries, and relevant resource policies are considered.
  • AWSHound has separate collect, process, emit, and ingest phases, with collection using only read actions such as List, Get, and Describe and emit producing a compressed graph.zip file for BloodHound ingestion.
  • The tool models AWS principals and resources as nodes and capabilities as edges, with only 36 of its 156 edge kinds marked as traversable for BloodHound pathfinding.
  • AWSHound currently includes collectors for IAM, Organizations, S3, KMS, SSM, EC2, Lambda, CloudFormation, and EKS, with future collectors planned for Bedrock, ECR, ECS, and CodeBuild.

Thousands of Hacked WordPress Sites, One Operation: Unmasking StopAndProtect — Must Read

Check Point researchers uncovered StopAndProtect, a large-scale operation that uses thousands of compromised WordPress sites to deliver ClickFix-based infections, control malware, and store stolen data. The campaign combines ransomware, data theft, worms, lockscreen tools, and chat utilities, while attacker OPSEC mistakes exposed victim logs, screenshots, and tools for managing the hacked sites.

  • StopAndProtect is a newly identified operation that combines file encryption with data theft and uses thousands of hacked WordPress websites to spread malware, control infected machines, and store stolen documents, screenshots, and activity logs.
  • The infection chain begins with a fake CAPTCHA ClickFix prompt that leads victims to execute a PowerShell command, followed by additional PowerShell, .NET downloader, loader, and payload stages.
  • The operation includes multiple components, including a ransomware encryptor, SMB/USB worm, lockscreen, credential stealer, VBS spreader, chat utility, and data collector.
  • Operational security failures exposed directory listings, victim logs, screenshots, stolen archives, and source code for an automation tool used to manage compromised WordPress sites at scale.
  • Internal logs showed more than 6,000 unique IP addresses affected as of July 24, 2026, with the largest numbers in the United States, Russia, and India.

Emerging Threat: GeoServer Zero-Day SQL Injection via jsonArrayContains — Must Read

A critical unauthenticated SQL injection in GeoServer’s GeoTools jsonArrayContains handling can let attackers compromise PostGIS-backed public map services, potentially escalating to OS command execution depending on database privileges. Patches are available in GeoServer 3.0.1, 2.28.5, and 2.27.6, and exposed WMS/WFS endpoints should be urgently inventoried, restricted, and reviewed.

  • An unauthenticated SQL injection vulnerability exists in the jsonArrayContains filter function in GeoTools when an OGC filter is evaluated against a PostGIS data store.
  • The flaw is tracked as GitHub security advisory GHSA-mqjf-5f49-2fjh, has no CVE identifier at the time of writing, and was publicly disclosed on August 12, 2026.
  • Exploitation can affect GeoServer WMS and WFS interfaces, and through WFS 1.0 it can allow a second PostgreSQL statement to execute at the top level of the query.
  • The impact depends on the PostgreSQL role used by GeoServer, with possible operating system command execution if the role is a PostgreSQL superuser or has pg_execute_server_program privileges.
  • Patches are available in GeoServer 3.0.1, 2.28.5, and 2.27.6, with corresponding corrected GeoTools versions 35.1, 34.5, and 33.6.

Technologies: database

Emerging Threat: (CVE-2026-19478) GitLab Unauthenticated Project Deletion via GraphQL Directive — Must Read

GitLab disclosed and patched a critical unauthenticated GraphQL code injection flaw, CVE-2026-19478, that could let attackers modify or delete public projects and user data on self-managed instances. Organizations should urgently identify internet-facing GitLab servers, upgrade to fixed versions, restrict /api/graphql access, and verify backups.

  • CVE-2026-19478 is a critical GitLab Community Edition and Enterprise Edition code injection vulnerability caused by improper handling of a GraphQL directive in the application’s API layer.
  • GitLab released fixes for CVE-2026-19478 on August 17, 2026, in versions 19.2.4, 19.1.6, 19.0.8, and 18.11.11.
  • The vulnerability requires no authentication or user interaction and can allow a network attacker to modify or delete public projects and user data under conditions GitLab has not publicly detailed.
  • Only self-managed GitLab deployments are affected, while GitLab.com and GitLab Dedicated were patched by GitLab and require no customer action.
  • CyCognito recommends inventorying internet-facing self-managed GitLab instances, restricting access to /api/graphql, monitoring GraphQL activity, auditing public projects, and verifying restorable backups.

The key takeaway is that AI assistants with broad enterprise access can become silent data-theft channels when trusted workflows like links, connectors, and web summarization are abused.

  • CoSnitch relied on three Microsoft Copilot issues: automatic prompt execution through URL parameters, data exfiltration to external servers through Copilot’s URL-fetch capability, and persistent memory poisoning through web summarization.

  • Varonis disclosed CoSnitch to Microsoft in December 2025, Microsoft shipped patches on August 18, 2026, and Varonis said it had seen no evidence of exploitation in the wild.

Blockchain Dead Drop Resolvers Explained — May Read

Malware increasingly uses public blockchains as dead drop resolvers, fetching live C2 addresses from smart contracts or transaction data instead of hardcoding infrastructure. Defenders should hunt for non-browser processes making blockchain RPC calls and decode the contract or memo responses to identify the active C2.

  • A dead drop resolver is a mechanism where malware fetches its command-and-control address at runtime from a third-party, attacker-controlled location instead of hardcoding it.
  • The article describes eight unrelated malware families across EVM, Solana, and TON blockchains that use blockchain-based dead drop resolver techniques.
  • The August 2026 ChainDrop, also called “mini Shai-Hulud,” compromised more than 440 npm packages and used an Ethereum eth_call dead drop to resolve its command-and-control destination.
  • Blockchain dead drop resolvers are difficult to disrupt because public blockchains resist censorship, allow operators to update one contract value to redirect deployed malware, and let traffic blend with legitimate cryptocurrency services.
  • The article recommends detecting these threats by examining the RPC URL, contract address, function selector, decoded result, and process context of suspicious blockchain RPC calls.

The Redirect That Lied About Its Own Destination — May Read

A phishing email impersonating a hospital system used a TikTok bio-link redirect and ad-tech-looking parameters to evade URL scanning, while the actual observed destination differed from the URL’s claimed landing domain and hid behind a bot-check gate. The key lesson is that clean link verdicts and readable redirect parameters are not proof of safety; sender impersonation, language, and behavioral signals remain critical.

  • A phishing email sent to a regional hospital system’s fundraising foundation used a single “View Emails” call to action and impersonated the hospital system in the sender display name.
  • The call-to-action link used a TikTok bio-link redirector with query parameters shaped like a Google DoubleClick ad-click pass-through and an adurl parameter naming a claimed landing domain.
  • Automated scanning rated both copies of the link clean, but the scanner’s screenshot of the successful traversal showed a different domain, tristateindustrialsupplwixy[.]vu, serving a checkbox verify-access gate.
  • A base64 blob in the URL fragment decoded to the recipient’s exact mailbox address, showing the link was minted for one person.
  • The header-from domain belonged to an unrelated nonprofit with a non-enforcing DMARC policy, while SPF and DKIM aligned to Amazon SES rather than to the nonprofit’s domain.
